replies.text:
No, this all began in 1935 when farm states successfully lobbied an "agricultural exemption" clause into the Motor Carrier Act of 1935, exempting agricultural trucking from ICC oversight.  As a result, the Teamsters failed to organize agricultural truckers.
Also, there was the Landrum–Griffin Act, which banned secondary boycotts, which crippled the Teamsters.
The Teamsters were highly opposed to trucking deregulalation.  Meanwhile, during the Oil Crisis, the agricultural truckers formed their own "craft" union and began lobbying in favor of deregulation.  Carter listened to the agricultural truckers instead of the Teamsters, and that ruined trucking for everyone.

comments.author: @tannerhancock5841
comments.text:
Okay, so I'm actually a Walmart PF driver myself, started back on the tail end of 2023 with their A2D program, Associate to Driver training to become a full time CDL driver.

For the pay side, yes, Walmart is very generous with their drivers, but also have high expectations due to that. We get bonuses every quarter based off how many miles we drove and keep track of our safe miles, the amount of miles driven consecutively without causing an accidnet or damages while driving. I'm only in year 3, and i've made 100k+ easily at 26, and i dont work that hard overall.

On the difficulty to get hired, yes, its is VERY difficult to get hired, because Walmart values safety over everything else. I remember being told the minimum requirements for OTR drivers to even QUALIFY to get tested is 250k safe miles and 3 years of experience. Then they give you tests on Pre-trip, backing, and driving (Rural, City, and Highway). Fail any of that 2 times, youre done and not getting the job.

For the Physical, its not a Company mandated one, its Federally mandated. Its to verify you arent suffering from any condition that could cause accidents, such as Narcolepsy, on any medications that could cause it, or that you dont have any major health issues that would make doing your job impossible. The major thing is for driver sleep, and if you have certain factors, such as a thick neck, theyll force you to use a CPAP machine that sends data on your usage to the company in case you dont use it, so they know youre getting proper rest before driving.

The tablets and dashcams are also a thing, and yes, it is for what they say and more. The tablet is used to track our locations and send truck data back to our shop if there are any issues. They dont normally track it live unless there is a major reason to. Most of the time, its usually to pinpoint the location of trucks on breakdown that need a tow. The cameras are set to trigger on specific things, such as hard braking, speeding, or anything deemed unsafe by Walmart. Its VERY useful cause some people try to commit insurance fraud, but it also catches drivers being unsafe before anything actually happens from their actions. 

Overall, Walmart IS considered the peak of a Driving job, due to them not constantly hounding you to rush loads, or do shady things while driving. They also pay pretty decently (not the top pay, since some companies pay 1+ dollars per mile), but they also give AMAZING benefits as one of the biggest companies involved with trucking.




From what I can understand about the Driver Shortage situation, its not entirely a myth. It has quite a few reasons on why it seems so.
1) Most companies dont treat their drivers with any sense of respect. They expect them to work like machines, pull illegal maneuvers that come back on the Driver over the company (i.e working in violation of hours or driving overweights).
2) Its an age thing as well. A LOT of the Driver community is 50+ in age from what I've seen, and im only 26. out of about 10-15 different Walmart DC's, and hundreds of drivers I see while working, I am almost always on the EXTREMELY low end in age. Its rare to find drivers under 40 alone, let alone under 30 in this day and age. So a lot of the drivers are starting to retire or such due to age.
3) Its people on the roads as well. I can't even count how many times i've almost been hit, witnessed major accidents, or seen road rage while working. Drivers in ANY vehicle these days are too selfish and ignorant to be worth driving around. I don't worry about my own driving NEAR as much as i'm concerned about whether some genius going 90+ playing on their phone is going to end up ending themselves by ramming my 80k lb tractor trailer.
4) Its also due to Company demands in this day and age. Companies are expected to be fast, no delays, and no issues for the consumer now, which just trickles down into all the rest of the company, so drivers are rushed and their needs are being ignored in comparison to the "lost profits" of the customers being unhappy with small delays.
5) Last but not least, its a grueling, unforgiving, and limiting job. You essentially sacrifice ALL your time to work. You work about 14 hours a day, 70 hours a week (thats if you go home afterwards when most companies dont do that) for your work. Thats time away from family, time relaxing and enjoying yourself, and more. You get AT MOST 2-3 days off normally every week, with no time after work unless you forgo about 100-200 extra dollars every day to shut down early. So for 5-6 days minimum, youre strapped to that truck working almost the entire time without a real break compared to any normal job that gets to go home after their day is done.

comments.author: @KeronWolf
comments.text: I drove trucks for three years, first under Schneider and then JB Hunt.  I've quit trucking due to bad job conditions that just wasn't worth the money.  First ran a dedicated route that was hourly pay ($30/hr) and that was something I was quite content with.  Then the company lost that account and I went into mileage OTR pay.  My pay declined down to the equivalent of $12/hr while working on average 55 hours a week (and bear in mind, NO MANDATORY OVERTIME for truckers).  Quit that job, went to a daycab job.  The good news there was getting home nightly so I didn't have to worry so much about parking and the pay was better but still mileage pay.  The bad was that I was now working 55-60 hours a week (technically it was 60-65 hours when adding in commute time to and from work) with still no OT compensation.  After a year of that I was fatigued to the point where I was driving almost entirely on autopilot and half the day I couldn't think straight.  Getting into an accident was the final straw and I haven't driven in a year.  The ONLY way I'll ever return to that damnable industry is two conditions: Hourly pay, and a 40-50 hour work week.
